rationale: A wins because it keeps four real doors open without pretending the supplied facts are richer than they are. Its best move is “How Brex built card issuing and local-currency reimbursement in 50 countries,” which gives a payments-infrastructure reporter an actual reporting path. B has usable material, but “Brex's 50-Country Push Is Also a $12.3 Billion Bet” wanders off into valuation pressure and revenue speculation the update did not give it. That is how you turn a launch into a finance fanfic with a blazer on.
gaps_in_A: “The finance team that stopped wiring reimbursements across borders” slightly overreaches: the update says local reimbursement, not that customers were wiring reimbursements before.
“the wires, the FX losses, the month-end mess” names pains that may be true, but they are not in the supplied facts; A wisely asks for proof, but the wording still decorates the hole.
A does not turn “top enterprise customer request” into a hard enough kill gate; without request-volume data, the enterprise-demand angle is still mostly Brex saying Brex heard a thing.
gaps_in_B: “Brex's 50-Country Push Is Also a $12.3 Billion Bet” is the big foul. The update gives a valuation and says profitability is undisclosed; it does not say valuation pressure, revenue growth, or costly infrastructure strain are live story facts.

“whether Brex's valuation can be sustained by revenue growth” invents an investor-pressure premise. A serious reporter can ask it, but PR should not pitch it as the angle without financial proof in hand.

“Corporate Cards Were a US Startup Story. Now the Software Is Going Everywhere.” is puffed-up category history. The update says Brex serves many venture-backed startups; it does not prove the whole category was a U.S. startup story.

Angle 1 and Angle 4 are too close: “traditional issuers have long owned” and “previously the exclusive domain of traditional financial institutions” are the same incumbent-versus-fintech story in different jackets.
